opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. My view is that even if the next breakthrough turns out to be quite disruptive, say a new architecture or a new learning paradigm beyond today's large models, you don't get there by skipping the current stage. Progress in this field has always been cumulative in a deeper sense than it looks from the outside.

First, the current approaches are how we learn what the real problems are. When we scaled up pretraining, we discovered things nobody predicted on paper: emergent abilities, but also very concrete limits in reasoning, long-horizon planning, and learning efficiency. Those limits are exactly what point toward the next paradigm. If you don't push the current method to its edge, you never see where the edge is.

Second, a lot of the infrastructure carries over even when the paradigm changes. Data pipelines, large-scale training systems, evaluation methods, the engineering know-how to run thousands of GPUs stably: these don't disappear. When the field shifted from CNNs to Transformers, the people who had built strong deep learning systems were the ones who could adopt Transformers fastest. The next shift will likely look similar.

Third, there's the practical side. The current generation is already useful. It creates real products and real value, and that funds the research and attracts the talent you need for the next leap. If everyone waited for the "perfect" method, there would be no ecosystem to support finding it.

And honestly, nobody knows for sure what the disruption will be or when it will come. Under that uncertainty, the reasonable strategy is to keep building seriously on what works now while keeping part of your effort on exploratory directions. Those two things aren't in conflict. Often the disruptive idea comes from people who understand the current paradigm deeply enough to see exactly where it breaks.

r001.rationale: The response says current approaches must be pushed to their edge to reveal their limits and real problems, which then guide the next paradigm.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is a question a lot of people in the field ask themselves quietly, especially those of us who have been through a few of these cycles already. And my honest answer is that you can't skip the current generation to get to the next one. The disruption, when it comes, is almost always built out of the practical knowledge that comes from pushing the present approach to its limits.

Think about what happened with vision. ResNet wasn't a bolt from the blue. It came out of years of people trying to train deeper networks, hitting the degradation problem, and understanding very concretely why it failed. The residual connection is a simple idea, but you only arrive at it after you have spent enough time inside the failure modes. If everyone had stood on the sidelines in 2013 saying "deep learning might be replaced by something better, let's wait," there would have been no accumulation of that experience, and the next step would not have happened either.

The same thing is true for large language models now. We don't fully understand why scaling works, where it stops working, what data actually matters, how reasoning emerges or fails to emerge. The only way to find out is to build the systems, run them at scale, and look carefully at what breaks. Every real limitation we discover is a signal pointing toward what the next paradigm needs to solve. If a future architecture replaces transformers, the people who design it will almost certainly be people who understood transformers very deeply, including their weaknesses.

There is also a more pragmatic point. The infrastructure, the data pipelines, the engineering culture, the evaluation methods, the talent, all of these carry over. Paradigms shift, but the organization that knows how to train a model on ten thousand GPUs, that has clean data and good tooling, that has people who can debug a divergent training run at three in the morning, that organization is in a much better position when the shift happens than one that waited.

So I actually see it the other way around. Working on today's approach is not in tension with the future disruption. It is the precondition for it. The thing I would warn against is not working on the current generation, but working on it without curiosity, just scaling for the sake of scaling and never asking why. If you keep asking why, you are already doing the work of the next generation.

r001.rationale: The response says the current approach must be pushed to its limits and its systems built and examined to discover what breaks, so its boundaries and problems can be understood.

astra-6.text:
I think the possibility of a disruptive advance doesn’t make the work we do today unnecessary. We don’t know when that advance will happen, or what it will depend on. It may come from discovering the limitations of current approaches, and you often have to push those approaches quite far before those limitations become clear.

There’s also value in what we can accomplish along the way. Current systems let us explore useful applications, learn what people actually need, and understand where reliability matters. Those lessons can remain valuable even if the underlying technology changes.

So I would keep developing today’s approaches while staying open to fundamentally different ideas. You can commit to making progress without assuming that the current path is the final one.

r001.rationale: The response says current approaches may need to be pushed quite far before their limitations become clear, directly conveying that maturing them helps reveal their boundaries and problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the possibility of a disruptive advance is a reason to keep exploring, but it isn’t a reason to stop working on what we have. We don’t know when that advance will happen, or which parts of today’s work it will build on. Developing current approaches helps us understand their strengths, discover their limits, and identify the problems a new approach needs to solve.

There’s also value we can deliver today. If we can make these systems more useful, reliable, and efficient, people benefit even before the next breakthrough arrives. So I see the two efforts as complementary: improve the methods we understand while leaving room to question their assumptions and pursue something fundamentally different.

r001.rationale: The response says developing current approaches helps reveal their strengths and limits, but it does not state that bringing them to sufficient maturity is necessary to fully understand their boundaries and problems.
